title: Two kinds of support for a causal claim: a difference between groups, and a mechanism

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A causal claim says that changing one thing, the exposure, changes another, the outcome.

Evidence of a difference between groups compares groups that differ in the exposure and asks whether the outcome differs between them. Other things equal, it is strongest when chance decided which group each person joined. Howick, Glasziou and Aronson (2009) call this direct evidence: evidence that an association between an exposure and an outcome is causal and not spurious, that is, not produced by chance, bias or a third factor.

Mechanistic evidence is evidence for the chain of steps by which the exposure is said to produce the outcome. Proposing a mechanism is not evidence that it operates.

A mechanism with no measured difference between groups is a hypothesis about the outcome, however well each step is understood. Howick and colleagues hold that mechanistic evidence should play a supporting role to direct evidence. They also name a third kind, parallel evidence: other studies, replications and similar ones, that give similar results.

Their three kinds are a regrouping of the considerations Austin Bradford Hill listed in 1965 for judging whether an association is causal.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
There are two ways to show that one thing causes another.

The first is to compare. Take two groups that differ in the thing, and see whether the result differs. Let chance decide who goes into which group.

The second is to explain how. Lay out the steps by which the thing would act in the body, and find evidence for each step.

Until someone compares groups and finds the difference, the story is a hypothesis.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
The section before this one showed that the breakfast claim rested on observational association. Its defenders also had a mechanism. Build it first, as an argument in the sense of Book 0’s section on argument (Book 0, F4): a chain of links, the claim the conclusion.

step link
1 Eating breakfast makes you less hungry later in the day.
2 So you eat less at lunch and afterwards.
3 So you eat less over the whole day.
4 Eating less over days and weeks lowers weight.
conclusion Eating breakfast lowers weight.

It reads well. Every step sounds like physiology. Now test each link, because each is a claim that needs its own evidence.

Brown and colleagues (2013) collected the short studies that measured these links. Their article is at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3798081/. Search it for “subsequent eating occasion”.

Although some studies showed a decreased energy intake at a subsequent eating occasion after eating compared with skipping breakfast, none of the studies showed a decrease in the sum of calories consumed across the study period when breakfast was eaten rather than skipped (Table 4).

So step 2 had some support. Step 3 had none. In two of the studies in their Table 4, by Kral and by Levitsky, total intake was higher when breakfast was eaten. In the second of Levitsky’s experiments, people who skipped breakfast ate more at lunch, but not enough to make up the breakfast they had missed. Brown and colleagues sum it up: “there is currently no clearly and consistently shown physiologic mechanism”.

Notice where the argument broke. Every link up to step 2 can hold and the conclusion still fail, because the breakfast itself can add more than eating less at lunch saves. A mechanism argument is a chain, and it is only as strong as its weakest link.

Now notice what the chain could never do on its own. Even with every link supported, it would tell you how breakfast might lower weight. It would not tell you that it does, or by how much, in real people living their lives. Only a comparison of groups can tell you that.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The studies of these links were short: in Brown’s Table 4, most lasted one day and the longest two. A link that fails over one day might hold over months, or the reverse. That is one reason a mechanism, however studied, cannot stand in for a measured difference in weight.

The four-step chain is this section’s own summary of the energy-intake mechanism Brown and colleagues describe. Other mechanisms were proposed, such as effects of the time of day on metabolism. Brown’s verdict covers those too.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now the other leg. Dhurandhar and colleagues (2014) compared groups whose breakfast advice was decided by chance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4095657/). Start with why that matters.

In an observational study, breakfast eaters choose to eat breakfast. They may differ from skippers in other ways that affect weight: sleep, work hours, activity, income. The trial’s authors say this in their introduction:

observational evidence does not preclude the possibility that breakfast eaters tend to weigh less because of other weight-related factors associated with breakfast eating.

Set out the comparison as an argument too.

step premise
1 The groups differ in the exposure: here, the breakfast advice.
2 The groups are alike in everything else that affects the outcome.
3 The outcome differs between the groups by more than chance alone would give.
conclusion The exposure changed the outcome.

If all three premises are true, the conclusion follows. In an observational comparison, premise 2 is the one in doubt, for the reason the trial’s authors give.

When chance decides the group, those other factors are spread between the groups by chance, not by choice. It uses the same tool as a random sample in Book 0’s section on sampling (Book 0, D6): an actual chance process, not a person, decides. Check that it worked. Search the trial’s Table 1 for “Weight (kg)”. The mean starting weights were 90.8 kg with general advice, 89.6 kg with advice to eat breakfast and 91.9 kg with advice to skip it.

91.9 minus 89.6 = 2.3

The three means lie within 2.3 kg of each other. The authors’ test of that gap gave P = 0.57: no difference beyond what chance gives. The groups started out close.

Now the result. Each person was told one of three things: general advice on healthy eating alone, the same plus “eat breakfast”, or the same plus “skip breakfast”. The authors also split them by their habit before the trial. Here are the mean weight changes over 16 weeks, in kg, for the 283 who completed it. A minus sign means weight went down. The authors adjusted each mean for starting weight, age, sex, site and race.

habit before the trial general advice only told to eat breakfast told to skip breakfast
usually skipped breakfast -0.71 -0.76 -0.61
usually ate breakfast -0.53 -0.59 -0.71

Compare the two breakfast arms (the trial’s groups) within each row. Among those who usually skipped breakfast, the group told to eat it lost a little more.

0.76 minus 0.61 = 0.15

Among those who usually ate breakfast, it went the other way: the group told to skip it lost a little more.

0.71 minus 0.59 = 0.12

Differences of 0.15 kg and 0.12 kg, in opposite directions. In both rows, those told to switch their habit lost a little more than the general-advice group, as the authors had predicted. But their test of all three arms together found no difference in weight larger than chance would explain (P = 0.77). Nor did the advice act differently on usual skippers and usual eaters beyond chance (P = 0.70).

Here premise 3 was not met. So by 2014 both legs were weak for this claim. The mechanism’s key link had not been shown. The one large comparison of groups made by chance found no detectable difference in weight.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Chance spreads other factors evenly on average, not in every trial. A small trial can be unbalanced by bad luck, which is why the authors’ Table 1 is worth checking, as you just did.

These are adjusted mean changes among completers, in adults with overweight or obesity trying to lose weight, at five sites, one of them in Copenhagen, over 16 weeks. The trial did not report a range of plausible values for the difference between arms, so read 0.15 and 0.12 kg as “small”, not as the true size of any effect.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
The opposite combination also happens: a strong difference between groups, with the mechanism unknown. Howick and colleagues give the classic case. Search their article (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2677430/) for “black box”.

For example, Doll and Hill’s famous study of the relation between the number of cigarettes smoked and the incidence of lung cancer38 did not refer in any way to what happens between inhalation of cigarette smoke and the development of tumours in the lung.

(The “38” run into the text is a reference number. Incidence means new cases in a period.) The study compared groups that smoked different amounts. The death rate from lung cancer in smokers was, as Howick and colleagues report it from Hill, “over 9 times the rate for non-smokers”. Later studies, which Howick and colleagues also cite, found that the risk fell when people stopped smoking: by half in those who stopped at age 50, and almost completely in those who stopped at age 30. That is a difference between groups too, run the other way.

Howick and colleagues count this comparison as good evidence of a cause, with no account of the steps inside the lung. That is the point of keeping the two legs apart. A missing mechanism does not cancel a strong difference. A strong mechanism does not supply a missing one.

The Hill of Doll and Hill is Austin Bradford Hill. In 1965 he set out a list of considerations for judging whether an association is a cause. Howick and colleagues regroup it into the kinds of evidence in this section. The list itself is taught at the next rung, the next level of this subject.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Smokers chose to smoke, so this comparison was observational, and a third factor could in principle have produced it. Howick and colleagues argue that a large effect can have “swamped the combined effects of any plausible confounders”, and that dose-response evidence is strongest “when the process is reversible”. A third factor would have to be linked to both smoking and lung cancer, more strongly than smoking is linked to lung cancer. It would also have to fall away when people stop. A small difference between self-chosen groups, like the breakfast association, carries far less weight. Size and design both matter, and weighing them is taken further in the next section.

points.html: “There is a clear mechanism, so it must work” is the error. The chain can hold at every link you tested and still fail at the outcome, because people can eat more later, as they did at lunch in the second of Levitsky’s experiments. Breakfast did lower lunch intake in some studies. No study showed lower intake over the whole day.

Was a difference in the outcome measured between groups that differ in the exposure, and who decided who was in which group? Is there evidence for each step of how it would work? Then say which leg is weak.
A study that measures one link, such as how much people eat at lunch, is not a study of the outcome, weight.
Do not advise a patient to change what they do on a mechanism alone. Say it is a hypothesis that has not been tested on weight.
“We know how it works” is not “we know it works”.
The two-leg check sorts evidence by kind. It does not weigh it.

When a resident cites Bradford Hill’s list as a checklist that proves a cause, stop them. Hill himself offered his points as viewpoints to consider, and the list is taught at the next rung. Here, ask only the two questions: is there a measured difference, and is there a shown mechanism?

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “The breakfast trial found no effect, so the mechanism was wrong.” Not necessarily. One link can be true, as the drop in lunch intake was in some studies. The outcome can still stay the same, because intake elsewhere in the day does not fall to match. The trial measured the outcome, not the links. A null comparison tells you the chain did not deliver a detectable change in weight under those conditions. It does not tell you which link failed.

blocks.label: Reporting it
blocks.html: The evidence that eating breakfast lowers weight is weak on both legs. The large trial that assigned breakfast advice by chance found no clear difference in weight. And no mechanism linking breakfast to a lower total daily intake has been consistently shown.

blocks.prompt: From memory: what are the two kinds of support for a causal claim? Which of the two can a claim not do without, if it is to be more than a hypothesis? And what is the third kind that Howick and colleagues add?
blocks.answer:
The first is a difference between groups. Compare groups that differ in the exposure, and see whether the outcome differs. It is best when chance decided the groups.

The second is a mechanism. Find evidence for each step of how the exposure leads to the outcome.

A claim cannot do without the first. With a mechanism alone, however good, it stays a hypothesis.

The third kind is parallel evidence: other studies that find the same thing.

blocks.prompt:
A slide in a postgraduate seminar on meal timing reads (made up for this exercise):

Late dinners cause obesity. The body handles food differently at night, so calories eaten late are more likely to be stored as fat.

You do not need to know whether the physiology is right. Say which leg of support the slide offers, which it leaves out, and what the slide may honestly claim.
blocks.answer:
The slide offers a mechanism. Its chain runs from eating late, to a change in how the body handles food at night, to more fat stored, to weight. Each link is a claim that needs its own evidence, and the slide gives none for any of them.

It leaves out any difference between groups. Do people who eat dinner late gain more weight than people who eat early? If they do, ask how that was found. In an observational comparison, late eaters may differ in sleep, shift work or income. In a trial, chance decides the timing.

An honest slide: “Eating late may change how the body handles food. Whether it changes weight has to be shown by comparing groups. That is a hypothesis to test, not yet a finding.”

blocks.prompt: Take the late-dinner claim from the last exercise. Specify the comparison that would test the difference-between-groups leg. Say who is compared, who decides which group each person is in, what is measured, and for how long. Then name one way your design could still mislead.
blocks.answer:
One sound design. Adults who agree to take part are split by a chance process, such as sealed numbered envelopes, into two groups. One group is asked to finish dinner by an early set time, the other to eat it late, with no other change to advice. Weight is measured at the start and after several months, by staff who do not know the group.

Chance deciding the group is the point: it spreads sleep, work hours and habits between the groups by chance, not by choice.

Ways it could still mislead (any one):

  • People may not follow the timing. Record whether they did.
  • People may eat more or less overall when told to change the timing. Then a difference in weight could come from the amount, not the timing.
  • A short trial may miss a slow effect. The breakfast trial’s own authors named its 16 weeks as a limit.
  • A small trial can be unbalanced by bad luck. Check the groups’ starting values.

blocks.prompt: For a first-year resident, ten minutes with a whiteboard. He says: “Breakfast reduces hunger at lunch, so of course it helps weight loss.” Use the breakfast evidence to show him the two legs and where each one stood by 2014.
blocks.answer:
Draw two columns: “difference between groups” and “mechanism”.

Under mechanism, write his chain: breakfast, less hunger, less at lunch, less over the day, lower weight. Then mark the links. Less at lunch: some short studies support it. Less over the whole day: none of the studies Brown and colleagues collected showed it, and two found more. The chain breaks at that link.

Under difference between groups, write two lines. Observational studies: breakfast skippers more often have overweight or obesity, but skippers may differ in other ways. The 2014 trial, where chance decided the advice: no detectable difference in weight over 16 weeks.

Then ask him which leg is weak. Both. His sentence is a hypothesis, and a fair one to test. It is not something to tell patients as fact.
